name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,893

clue.text: Ability to calculate shower pressure in boudoir

indicators.note: One thing put in another ends up surrounded by it, so the two pieces named before this word are planted inside the room named after it.

blocks.note: a bower is a lady's private room, which is what boudoir means, and it splits open after its first letter
a shower of rain, read as weather rather than as plumbing
P is the standard symbol for pressure in physics

explanation.walkthrough: The bathroom is the trap: 'shower pressure in boudoir' reads as one plumbing complaint, and not a word of it is doing that job.
explanation.definitionFit: Ability to calculate -> BRAINPOWER: brainpower is raw mental capacity, and working sums out in your head is the everyday demonstration people mean by it.

clue.text: Gift from fiancé on vacation, the traditional one

indicators.note: A word sent on vacation is emptied out, and all that stays behind to mind the place is its first letter and its last.

blocks.note: a present from someone is a present of theirs, so this preposition swaps for its two-letter twin
only the outer pair survives the emptying, and the accented é is read as a plain E
on getting engaged, the traditional thing to hand over is a ring

explanation.walkthrough: The engagement story is doing double duty: the ring genuinely is the traditional gift, so the last piece of the wordplay and the surface picture are the same object.
explanation.definitionFit: Gift -> OFFERING: an offering is a thing presented — at an altar, in tribute, or to a host — so it is a gift seen from the giver's side.

clue.text: High ground dropped away

blocks.note: up north a bare moorland hill goes by this word — Scafell and Bowfell carry it in their names
the past tense of fall, said of land sloping down or of a level dropping

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it sounds like a landslip, and it is two unrelated senses. The northern hill is the half a solver outside Britain is least likely to have met.
explanation.definitionFit: High ground -> FELL is a northern English moorland hill; dropped away -> FELL is the past tense of fall, as land or prices fall away.

clue.text: Finding book for kids excited Welsh lawyer

indicators.note: Something excited will not sit still, and letters that will not sit still end up in an order other than the one handed to you.

blocks.note: eleven letters, exactly what the two-part enumeration asks for

explanation.walkthrough: A Welsh lawyer is a person, not a piece of machinery, which is what makes the surface hold — the letter count is the only thing marking the phrase as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Finding book for kids -> WHERE'S WALLY: the British name of the Where's Waldo picture books, in which children hunt one striped figure hidden in a vast crowd.

clue.text: Mother in stable steps in dirt according to Spooner

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner's trick was swapping the opening sounds of two words, so what you say and what you write begin each other's way round.

blocks.note: dirt is mud, and after the swap its M has gone next door and an ST has arrived in exchange
steps are a stair, and with its ST traded away it takes the M and is written out to match the sound

explanation.walkthrough: A mother in a stable pulls hard towards the nativity, and there is no manger here at all — the stable is a horse's and the mother is a breeding animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Mother in stable -> STUD-MARE: at a stud farm the stud-mare is the animal kept for breeding, so being a mother in a stable is her entire job.

clue.text: Republican in crooked club means to straighten out

indicators.note: A letter said to be in something is simply one of its letters, so the Republican's initial joins the pile waiting to be rearranged.
Crooked means bent out of true, and letters bent out of true no longer stand in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: R is the letter printed beside a Republican politician's name in American usage
nine more letters of fodder, taken exactly as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Means to' reads as joinery announcing the definition, and the letter count is what gives it away: 'means' supplies five of the ten letters being shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: to straighten out -> UNSCRAMBLE: to unscramble a thing is to put a jumble back into order, which is straightening it out in the figurative sense.

clue.text: Velvety fabric nearly quality that's desirable

indicators.note: Nearly a whole word is all of it bar the final character, so the fabric's name stops one letter short of finishing.

blocks.note: plush is the deep-piled velvety cloth, and it hands over everything except its closing H

explanation.walkthrough: Four words that read as one sentence about upholstery, and 'nearly' is the hinge: it belongs to the fabric behind it, not to the quality in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: quality that's desirable -> PLUS: a plus is a point in something's favour, the advantage you list when weighing one option against another.

clue.text: Spinning round?

blocks.note: the surface offers a pirouette or a wheel turning; a bullet spins too, because of the spiral grooves cut inside a gun barrel
a round is a single cartridge, and the question mark is the setter admitting these two words name one object

explanation.walkthrough: Rifling is the spiral cut inside a barrel, and it spins the bullet so that it flies true. Read 'round' as ammunition rather than as a shape and the clue is one picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinning round? -> RIFLE SHOT: the whole clue is the definition, since a round fired from a rifle leaves the barrel spinning, which is what rifling is for.

clue.text: Post just arrived left on end of table

indicators.note: In an across entry a piece laid on another goes after it, so the letter named before this word lands to the right of the one named after.
The end of a word is the letter it finishes with, so all that is wanted here is one closing character.

blocks.note: something that has just arrived is new
TABLE gives up its closing letter and nothing else
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.walkthrough: 'Post' pulls towards the mail and 'just arrived' keeps that delivery picture going. Nothing in the surface survives the parse — the answer is a piece of joinery.
explanation.definitionFit: Post -> NEWEL: a newel is the stout post at the foot or head of a staircase that carries the handrail, so it is a post by trade.

clue.text: See 4
Model observed fish using ears

indicators.note: Ears hear rather than read, so the two words beside this are to be judged by their sound and not by how they are spelt.

blocks.note: observed is EYED and a fish is an EEL; run the pair together and one quite differently spelt word comes out

explanation.walkthrough: Say the two words quickly and the join between them disappears, which is the whole device — 'using ears' is the only thing telling you to stop reading and start listening.
explanation.definitionFit: Model -> IDEAL: a model pupil is an ideal one, the adjective sense meaning perfect of its kind rather than the noun for someone on a catwalk.

clue.text: Clear sporting clue is for guys

indicators.note: Sporting is playing about, and letters played about with come out in an order other than the one they arrived in.

blocks.note: to clear a place of something is to rid it of that thing
six letters shaken into a new order and parked behind the first three

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clear' looks like the definition and turns out to be the first three letters. The definition is the last word, and it has to be read as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: guys -> RIDICULES: to guy someone is to mock them publicly, the fairground sense that gave the Guy Fawkes effigy its name.

clue.text: Charges covering any number of people like Andrew in the past

definitions.text: people like Andrew in the past

indicators.note: Something covering another thing lies over it on both sides, so the word before this closes around the letter named after it.

blocks.note: what a shop charges are its prices, and the word opens up after three letters
N is the mathematician's letter for a number left unspecified

explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges covering' wants to be a verb about accusations, which is what makes the sentence read as a news bulletin rather than as a price list.
explanation.definitionFit: people like Andrew in the past -> PRINCES: definition by example, and 'in the past' does real work — Andrew was styled a prince until the title was given up.

clue.text: Charlie driving across fields perhaps promising party

blocks.note: Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet, the one pilots and police spell with
anyone driving across fields is perhaps on a tractor, and those words are written down as they are said

explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie driving' reads as one person at a wheel, and the split falls between the two words: one is a single letter, the other a picture to be named.
explanation.definitionFit: promising party -> CONTRACTOR: in law a party to a contract is one who has promised to perform, so the firm you hire is the promising party.

clue.text: Therapist at gathering votes against admitting learner

indicators.note: A gathering draws things into itself, so the short word before it closes around everything named next.
To admit someone is to let them in through the door, so the letter after this word goes inside the word before it.

blocks.note: the two letters are taken as they stand and then pulled apart to make room
a nay is a vote against, and the plural splits after two letters
L is the plate a learner driver must display in Britain

explanation.walkthrough: Three small words do all the work and none of them looks like wordplay. The trap is reading 'at gathering' as a place rather than as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Therapist -> ANALYST: the analyst meant is a psychoanalyst, a therapist by profession, not the sort who works on spreadsheets.

clue.text: Hotel in Goa boiling? God, I know!

definitions.note: This is a line spoken by the answer rather than a synonym for it: the setter defines the person by what that person would claim, so it cannot be swapped into a sentence as a noun.

indicators.note: Water at a rolling boil throws everything in the pot around, and letters treated that way settle into a new arrangement.

blocks.note: ten letters, exactly the length wanted, taken as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: Goa is a holiday coast, so the first half reads as a complaint about the heat. Nothing here is an abbreviation — all ten letters go straight into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: God, I know! -> THEOLOGIAN: knowing about God is the whole of the job, so the exclamation is the claim the qualification entitles you to make.

clue.text: Truck came first loaded with silver

indicators.note: A cart loaded with something has it sitting inside, so the letters named after this go within the word in front of it.

blocks.note: whoever came first in the race won it, and the word opens after one letter
AG is the chemical symbol for silver, from the Latin argentum

explanation.walkthrough: The race picture runs right through the clue, and the medal is the joke: silver here is the element on the periodic table, not second place.
explanation.definitionFit: Truck -> WAGON: on the railway a truck is a wagon, the open freight sense rather than the road vehicle most readers picture first.

clue.text: One already mentioned mother's embraces

definitions.note: The answer is an article, not a noun: 'one already mentioned' describes the job this little word does — pointing back at something both speakers have met — rather than standing in for it in a sentence.

indicators.note: An embrace closes round whatever is held, so a run of letters is being kept inside a word rather than spelled out for you.

blocks.note: three consecutive letters sit inside this word, starting at its third

explanation.walkthrough: Tiny answers hide in plain sight, and 'mother's' is the only word here with room for one. The definition is a grammar lesson: the definite article points back at something already introduced.
explanation.definitionFit: One already mentioned -> THE: the definite article marks a noun the listener has already met, which is exactly what separates it from 'a'.

clue.text: Bath covered with hair gives offence

indicators.note: Something covered with a thing has it laid over the top and round the sides, so the word after this closes over the word before it.

blocks.note: a tress is a long lock of hair, and it splits after three letters
Bath is the English city built on hot springs, and a spa is what such a place is

explanation.walkthrough: The capital B does the misleading: this is the Somerset city rather than a tub, and 'gives' is only joinery between the wordplay and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: offence -> TRESPASS: in law a trespass is a civil wrong, and in older religious English a sin — 'forgive us our trespasses' — so either sense offends.

clue.text: Green surface of parking spaces reported

indicators.note: A word reported is passed on by mouth, so what matters is how the phrase before it sounds and not how it is written.

blocks.note: a parking bay is a marked space, and the plural said aloud is spelt another way entirely

explanation.walkthrough: The green is snooker's, not a golf course or a village lawn — this puzzle keeps returning to the game, and this is the cloth it is played on.
explanation.definitionFit: Green surface -> BAIZE: baize is the coarse woollen cloth, dyed green, stretched over snooker and card tables, so it is a green surface by trade.

clue.text: Setter's opposed to editor's thought

blocks.note: the setter is the person who wrote the puzzle, so 'setter's' comes out as I'm
agin is the dialect spelling of against, as in agin the government
ED is the usual short form for an editor, and the apostrophe-s after it only holds the sentence up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' is the convention worth keeping: it names the person writing the clue, so I, me and I'm are all in play wherever the word appears.
explanation.definitionFit: thought -> IMAGINED: in the past tense the two swap freely — 'I thought I heard something' and 'I imagined it' both report a picture in the mind.

clue.text: Official dealing with loose pockets back in time

indicators.note: To pocket a thing is to slip it inside and keep it there, so the letter named next is buried in the word before it.
The back of a word is the letter it finishes with, so only one closing character is taken from the word beside it.

blocks.note: re at the head of a memo means concerning, or dealing with
an animal that is loose is free, and the word opens after one letter
only TIME's closing letter is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose pockets' reads as one phrase about baggy trousers and is two instructions: the loose thing is what does the pocketing.
explanation.definitionFit: Official -> REFEREE: the official in charge of a match is the referee, and snooker keeps one standing at the table all through a frame.

clue.text: Large breaks show talent

indicators.note: Something breaking into a word forces its way through the middle, leaving the two halves either side of it.

blocks.note: a fair is a show — a trade fair, a county fair — and it splits after one letter
L is the size printed on a clothing label for large

explanation.walkthrough: The snooker sense of 'breaks' is what the surface is selling. Here the word is an instruction, and 'show' has to be read as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: talent -> FLAIR: flair is a natural talent for something, carrying the extra sense of doing it stylishly rather than merely well.

clue.text: Line you wait for, to shout out loud "4D 18A ___ 25A?"

definitions.note: The definition is a fill-in-the-blank rather than a synonym: solve the three numbered entries, read the question they spell out, and the answer is the word missing from it.

indicators.note: What is said out loud is heard rather than read, so the word before it hands over its sound and not its spelling.

blocks.note: an actor waits for a cue, the line that tells them to speak
to bawl is to shout at full volume, and once you have only the sound it is spelt this way

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gaps and the quotation is a snooker commentator's catchphrase, asked while the white rolls on after the strike.
explanation.definitionFit: "4D 18A ___ 25A?" -> CUE BALL: the missing word completes 'Where's the cue ball going?', the white that a player strikes and then watches travel.

clue.text: A hundred and two sailors share the bill

blocks.note: C is a hundred in Roman numerals
an ordinary seaman is an OS in the Navy and an old hand at sea is a tar, and the two are written one after the other

explanation.walkthrough: 'Share the bill' looks like splitting a restaurant tab, which is the whole joke — the bill meant is the poster outside a theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: share the bill -> CO-STAR: two actors who co-star are billed together above the title, so sharing the billing is precisely what the verb describes.

clue.text: Frames featuring the blue?

blocks.note: in snooker a frame is one complete game, which is the reading the surface wants; a frame is also what a painting hangs in
on a table the blue is a ball; in a gallery it is water, and a picture of water is mostly water

explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle has been playing snooker throughout, so 'frames' and 'the blue' land on the table first. Take them into a gallery instead and the answer is a wall of pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: Frames featuring the blue? -> SEASCAPES: the whole clue is the definition, since these are framed pictures whose subject is the blue open water.

clue.text: Put money by bar

blocks.note: putting money by is what you do with whatever you have not spent
the preposition meaning except, as in 'all bar one' — nothing to do with drink

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are everyday words and neither is the pub: 'bar' is the preposition meaning except, and the answer carries that same sense in 'all save one'.
explanation.definitionFit: Put money by -> SAVE, the banking sense of setting money aside; bar -> SAVE, the formal preposition meaning except, as in 'all save one'.

clue.text: On and off

definitions.note: Neither definition matches the answer's part of speech: both are the short adverbs that stand in for it in speech, since a machine still on is still going and a person who is off is going.

blocks.note: a match that is still on is still being played, and an engine on is running
'I'm off' is what you say as you leave, so this is departure rather than continuation

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, one answer twice over. The clue works because 'on and off' is itself a phrase, and that is what stops you splitting it into halves.
explanation.definitionFit: On -> GOING, as an engine or a party still running; off -> GOING, as in 'I'm off' — the answer covers both continuation and departure.

clue.text: Down under ginger's first to turn red, perhaps

indicators.note: In a down entry whatever is under something is written below it, so the word before this instruction ends up beneath the letter after it.
A word's first is the single character it begins with, so ginger surrenders one letter and keeps everything else.

blocks.note: ginger gives up its opening letter and nothing else
low means down, as in low spirits or a low ceiling

explanation.walkthrough: 'Down under' is Australia in the surface and two separate pieces in the parse, and 'ginger' is a hair colour there rather than a spice.
explanation.definitionFit: turn red, perhaps -> GLOW: cheeks that glow are flushed red with warmth or embarrassment, and 'perhaps' concedes that glowing can be any colour.

clue.text: Sign name for 17 18 & 19 across

blocks.note: the zodiac reading — one of the twelve star signs, the one running from late August
those three answers run together as a wag on the baize, a joker at the snooker table, and one man made his name being exactly that

explanation.walkthrough: Read 17, 18 and 19 across as one phrase and the answer is John Virgo, the snooker player turned commentator whose catchphrase 23 across quotes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sign -> VIRGO: a zodiac sign, and also the surname of John Virgo, the snooker entertainer that row of the grid describes as a wag on the baize.

clue.text: ... thus time takes a popular TV institution

indicators.note: One thing that takes another swallows it whole, so the pieces named after this word go inside the two already laid down.

blocks.note: so means thus, the plainest substitution in the clue
the article goes in as the single letter it is
pop is the everyday short form of popular, as in pop music
an era is a stretch of time

explanation.walkthrough: The three dots carry the surface on from 26 across and do no work at all, while 'time takes' looks like a proverb and is really two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: TV institution -> SOAP OPERA: the long-running daily serial is one of television's fixtures, so this is an institution by example rather than by dictionary synonym.
